title: The key that cracked the hieroglyphs
text: For fourteen centuries the writing of ancient Egypt was a closed book: nobody could {{1}} hieroglyphs, and the civilisation that built the pyramids kept its thoughts to itself. The {{2}} came in 1799, when French soldiers digging a fortification near the Nile town of Rosetta hit a slab of dark stone carved with the same text three times — in hieroglyphs, in everyday demotic script, and in Greek. Scholars could read the Greek {{3}}, which meant the other two versions now had a known meaning to be matched against them. Even so, the code took twenty years to {{4}}. Thomas Young made the first inroads, showing that a group of signs wrote the name Ptolemy inside a royal ring; Jean-Francois Champollion went further in 1822, {{5}} the sound values of the signs and demonstrating that hieroglyphs wrote a living language, not merely pictures. The stone itself never left British hands — it had been {{6}} by the army that defeated the French in Egypt — and it has stood in the British Museum since 1802, one of the most visited objects in London. Modern curators are uneasy about such {{7}}, and Egypt has repeatedly asked for the stone's return. Whatever the outcome, the intellectual debt is settled: everything we know of Egyptian administration, medicine and belief {{8}} on that single accidental find.

gaps.explanation: 'nobody could decipher hieroglyphs' — decode the writing; despise, demolish and betray share the de- shape but reject, destroy or give away.
'The breakthrough came in 1799' — the decisive advance; breakdown = collapse, breakage = damage, breakout = escape.
'could read the Greek version' — the Greek form of the same text; vision = sight, division = separation.
'took twenty years to crack' — the standard verb for solving a code; the near-forms do not collocate with codes.
'establishing the sound values of the signs' — determining them conclusively; abolish and demolish mean destroy, nourish = feed.
'it had been seized by the army' — captured; cease = stop, sieve = strain, size = measure.
'uneasy about such acquisitions' — museum purchases; inquisition = harsh interrogation, quotation = a cited phrase.
'rests on, is founded on, that accidental find' — founded on = based on; fund = finance, flounder = struggle.
